tasks.short: Check the structure and hidden embers, agree the handover with the officer and owner, and fill in the handover form.

steps.what: Firefighter inspects fire sites for collapse risk after flames have been extinguished
Firefighter checks for hidden embers with a thermal camera
Firefighter discusses remaining danger with the officer and the owner before handover
Firefighter writes address, time and unit on the paper handover form
Firefighter notes the site state and handover on the form

tasks.design: The handover form on the truck's tablet in the safety region's incident system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) fills address, time and unit from the control-room record, and the firefighter notes the site state and handover with pick lists. Checking the structure, finding embers and talking with the owner stay fully on site.
tasks.previous_blocker: Handover forms were paper, with details copied from the alarm.
tasks.enabler_now: Control-room records hold times, address and units for every incident.
tasks.still_hard: Judging that a site is safe is experience; the form only records it.
tasks.human_edge: Feeling that a floor will not hold before stepping on it.

reach.learn: Whether prefilled forms cut errors in handovers.

evidence.claim: Control-room data give response time per phase for every safety region.
Public bodies must keep records in good, orderly and accessible state.

assumptions: Boundary: from the extinguished fire to the recorded handover; investigation is outside.
Input contract: control-room record from the safety region's control room; form fields set by the region's information manager; fallback is paper.
Site checks and talks do not change.
unknowns: Incidents with a formal handover per month.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Almost all of this task is checking the site.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Scan the burned area for heat, walk to each suspect spot, dig out and wet hot spots, mark checked sections and report the area clear.

steps.what: Firefighter patrols burned areas with a hand-held thermal camera to locate hot spots
Firefighter walks to each suspect spot and checks it
Firefighter digs out and wets hot spots to eliminate them before they restart fires
Firefighter marks checked sections on a paper map
Firefighter reports the area clear to the officer by radio

tasks.design: A drone with a thermal camera, flown by the region's drone pilot, scans the burned area and marks suspect heat on the map on the truck's tablet ({OPS_SYSTEM}), replacing the slow sweep with a hand-held camera. Firefighters walk to each mark, check and extinguish it, and tick sections on the tablet map; reporting clear stays by radio.
tasks.previous_blocker: Hot spots were found by walking the whole area with a hand-held camera.
tasks.enabler_now: Thermal drones are used by fire services to survey large areas.
tasks.still_hard: Drones miss heat under thick cover; the final check is on foot.
tasks.human_edge: Smelling smoke that no camera has picked up.

reach.learn: Whether thermal maps shorten after-fire patrols.

evidence.claim: Fire services use drones with thermal cameras to survey large burned areas.
Drone images can show people; flights over private land must respect privacy rules.

assumptions: Boundary: from the burned area to the area reported clear; firefighting itself is outside.
Input contract: drone flights by the region's drone pilot; map layer from the incident system; fallback is the hand-held sweep.
Checking and extinguishing do not change.
Drone pilot time is outside the firefighter's savings.
unknowns: How many incidents have large burned areas.
research_questions: Do re-ignitions fall after drone scans?

incremental.description: Drone pilot flies the thermal survey.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Small fires, or no drone available, keep the full walk.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Get times and units from the control room, debrief the crew, write the narrative, record casualties and damage, have the commander sign and send the report to the archive.

steps.what: Firefighter copies times, address, units and alarm class from the control-room log
Firefighter debriefs with the crew to gather the facts
Firefighter prepares the written narrative that details specifics of the fire incident

loop.input: The recorded crew debrief, made with the crew's agreement, and the prefilled report header.
loop.output: A draft narrative of what the crew found and did, in the region's report order.
loop.check: Code checks that every time, address and unit in the draft matches the control-room record and that no victim names or injuries appear in the narrative field; the firefighter edits the draft; no unreviewed text leaves the record.
loop.stop: One draft per incident; on failure the firefighter writes it.
loop.why_not_simpler: A debrief is free talk; a form cannot turn it into a readable account.

steps.what: Firefighter records casualties and damage
Crew commander checks, assembles and signs the incident report
Firefighter e-mails the signed report to the region's archive

tasks.design: The incident report in the safety region's incident system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) fills times, address, units and alarm class from the control-room record. A bounded step drafts the narrative from the recorded crew debrief, checked against that record, and the firefighter edits it; casualties and damage go into restricted fixed fields. The crew commander owns the report: checks the parts, assembles and signs it, and only then does the system file it in the archive.
tasks.previous_blocker: Reports were typed in documents with data copied from the control-room log.
tasks.enabler_now: Control-room data per incident are digital, and language models can draft a narrative from a recorded talk.
tasks.still_hard: Drafts can misstate what happened; reports can matter in court and insurance.
tasks.human_edge: Writing what the crew actually saw, including what went wrong.
tasks.altitude: The firefighter edits drafts; the crew commander still signs.

reach.learn: Whether structured reports make analysis easier.

evidence.claim: Control-room data give response time per phase for every safety region.
About half the 2019 to 2023 rise in residential fire alerts reflects better registration, not more fires.
Injury details are health data under the GDPR.
Voice logs that show crew performance need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from the incident record to the archived report; investigations are outside.

Input contract: control-room record from the safety region's control room; report order and fields set by the region's information manager; debrief recorded with the crew's agreement; fallback is typing.
Debrief recordings are deleted once the report is signed and are not used to judge crews.
Crew commander time is outside the firefighter's savings.
unknowns: Whether the works council agrees to debrief recording.
research_questions: How often does the commander change the edited narrative?

incremental.description: Firefighter starts and stops the debrief recording.
Information manager audits samples of reports.

approvals.approved_version: The incident report as signed by the crew commander in s5; any change needs a new signature before filing.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Complex incidents need long narratives that drafts help with less.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Work with police on scene, preserve evidence, give statements, select photos and the report for police and send them securely.

steps.what: Firefighter collaborates with police to respond to accidents and disasters on scene
Firefighter preserves evidence and points out signs of arson to investigators
Firefighter answers investigators' questions by phone later
Firefighter selects photos and the report for the arson investigation
Firefighter e-mails photos and the report to the police

tasks.design: Photos taken on the truck's tablet are stored with the incident in the safety region's incident system ({OPS_SYSTEM}); on a police request the firefighter selects files, and the system shares them through a secure, logged link instead of e-mail. Working with police on scene, preserving evidence and answering questions stay as they are.
tasks.previous_blocker: Photos sat on phones and cameras and were e-mailed in batches.
tasks.enabler_now: Incident systems store media per incident and share it through logged links.
tasks.still_hard: Photos can show victims; sharing needs a legal basis and a log.
tasks.human_edge: Noticing the detail at the scene that points to arson.

reach.learn: Whether linked files arrive faster and complete.

evidence.claim: Incident systems can store media per incident and share it through logged links.
Photos showing injuries are health data under the GDPR.

assumptions: Boundary: from the joint response to files shared; the police investigation is outside.
Input contract: police requests come through the region's liaison officer; sharing rules set by the region's privacy officer; fallback is e-mail.
Police time is outside the firefighter's savings.

incremental.description: Firefighter uploads scene photos to the incident after the call.

approvals.approved_version: The files selected by the firefighter in s4 for this request; other files need a new selection.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Most of this task is on scene.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The firefighter keeps every judgement on scene; copying, typing and e-mailing around incidents shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A firefighter whose report is ready to sign before the truck is back in the station.
